MUTUAL ASSISTANCE SOCIE'I Y Of the Reformed Dutch Church. We have often in our columns urged the formation of Provident societies, and are extremely happy to learn that the society formed by the members of the Dutch Reformed congregation, under the above title is progressing even more rapidly than its most sanguine well wishers anticipated þÿ we are extremely happy to find that although the Institution was especially designed for the benefit of the members of the Reformed Dutch congregation, that individuals ot another communion aie eligible if of good and moral character þÿ this is in a true chistiau spirit, for a provision against sickness or to afford the means for decent burial should be open to all deserving objects. The rules of the society are published, and are in general unexceptionable þÿ but ! one article viz , the 14th, appears to us, to be rather arbitrary for it is as follows. In order to preserve the respectability of this society, all cases of bad conduct in any of its members shall be reported to the Pastor, u>ao may admonish the offender, and if necessary exclude the transgressor, Jrom the society. The above rule appears to us to require revision on principle þÿ we do not lor a moment imagine, or cun have the most remote idea of insinuating lhal any minister of itie gospel, would not in such a case, act conscientiously, or that he would not candy and deliberately investigate the tiuih or falsehood of anv charge brought against an erring member of his flock þÿ yet ! we think that the ofletuier ought to be tried by a jury of his

peers, alias a committee chosen fiom t he members of the society, and that the pastor then should admonish or expel the tiansgressor according to the decision of the committee. In making the foiegoing remarks, we are actuated by no sinister motive for we sincerely wish the society prosperity, and are confident that very many will live to bless the hour in which they joined it, for in tropi. cal climates health is so precarious t fiat every prudent individual should provide against such a contingency. þÿ and surely when stricken by the angel of death, it must soothe the sufferers dying hour to know that they will be decently buried, and that the last rites of our holy and sacred religion will be secured to them.

India. þÿ The India mail, which has just arrived, brings leiters and papers from Bombay up to the 1st of April ; that is, by a passage scarcely of live weeks, instead of the six months' duration o( former periods, iso much has steam changed the local and political relations of kingdoms. These mails have been ex peeled with an interest much beyond their intrinsic importance under the circumstances ot the recent proceedings of the Board of Directors for the recall of Lord Ellenborough, arid the implied reveisai of his system of policy þÿ Conquer all you can, extend your empire, and confirm all your existing influence, þÿ is the uniform language of Loid Elicnborough and in the consistent prosecution of this policy, the first article of intelligence contained in these mails declares that .Semite is finally and for ever annexed to the Biiiisfi þÿpossessions. On the other part, the language of the Board of Directors is to restore and maintain general peace ; to keep their empire within its former boundaries, and not to engage in such wars, political intrigues, and in the gathering and keeping up of overawing armies, þÿ the cost of which must necessarily consume the revenue of the Indian empire, and exhaust and impoverish the genciai wealth of the Company

It is ol course as vet unknown inoiigsi the totally unknown iri (he supreart - coined, that public in India, though we s sp<ct not so Luid Ellenborough has been recalled. As it appears by the Duke of þÿWellington speech s in the Lotds on Monday that the Board of Dircctois and the government had been in correspondence on this subject for nearly six months, and as any single period of six weeks during this half year would be sufficient to enable any single director of the Boatd to communicate the intelligence of this put pose to any of bis friends in India, it is certainly a very leasonable inference that tins design of the Boatd to recall the Governor General is as well known amongst the higher officers in India as in England, and of course by Lord Ellenborough himself. Indeed, we have a very strong suspicion, that the complete and thorough evacuation of Gwalior, and the plenary restoration of the Rajah, together wiih the instant return of the army from that district towards Calcutta. haie been produced by these known sentiments of the Board of Directors; that Lord Ellenborough found he Lad gone too far for the wishes of his masters, whom we suspect he treated with a little neglect and indifference, and tfiat a backward siep had become necessat v. There is nothing of this, however, in the papers before us. Ihe extraordinary proceedings in England, as we have above said, ate as vet wholly unknown bv the Indian press and public, however different the matter may be as regards the supreme council and higher officers.

Accordingly, by the last accouma from India, Lord Ellenborough is every where received with a popular favour and distinction which wait upon success. He everywhere moves forward as in a car of triumph and, as always happens amongst n ankiud, const) ictos gloria cun u, þÿ he draws the people with him n shouting train after ins wheels. So striking is Ihe vicissitude of human affairs, and into s.icli errors and blindness are men led by those secret and unknown circumstances which remain yet concealed to them in tne womb of time and remoteness Thus, w hilst Lord Ellenborough is actually recalled by bis masters in England, one Indian town after another is getting up its fete to nail and receive the successlul conqueroi of his day. The intelligence from China amounts to nothing hut that tranquillity continues, and that the Chinese are availing themselves of the present state of things to raise the price ol their teas, and to supply them in such limited qualities as to enforce this tuciease. þÿ This mischief, however, must necessarily pass away under the necessary effect of the magnitude ol this staple of China, and under the common exigency of the Chinese as well as ourselves to deal in this article. We might as well appieheud a monopoly of American cottou as a monopoly m the China tea market.

The Inst article in these papers is so singularly at variance with what is going on in England that we shall give it in tne words of the India paper þÿ The popularity of Lord Ellenborough ap pears to be on the increase in Calcutta, where a public meeting was called by the sheriff for the purpose of addressing bis lordship on ins return f loin the campaigns in Gwalior, 'ihe newspa|«r readers of Bombay cannot fail to have observed the silence of the violent assailants of itie policy of his lordship. To the Editor ol the St. Thomas Times. þÿSir, Having lately visited the different islands on die West Coast of Africa, from vCurnim Guano is obtained, nn article now ira Inirti repute in England þÿ I hereby enclose vou a brief description of them presuming that it may prove inleresiing to many of your renders. The tirsl of the afoiesmd islands is named Possession and is m la r. 20 5i S from which, however, but very Imie Guano has been obtained the article being impure. 'Hus island presents a most (m bidding and repulsive aspect þÿ one ai wimhibe nund recoiis wnb horror, appearing as having been designed neither for the use or benefit ol man or brine, but that it had sprang into existence through some of þÿnature svvHd freaks, the vomiting of some subterranean hre it js one dreary waste of parched sand, not a tree, shrub, or bush meets Hie eve to 1 fill ven the scene, and to judge from external evidences, but lew ol the feathered mho n,>w resort to ii. Seais have however been taken here in great numbers to judge from the immense quantities of bones strewed upon its barren surface, as though it showed instinct in selecting this void in creation, as one of their numerous þÿhaunts, Vet ! man always active, and alive in the pursuit of gain has followed and swept them from the island. A most singular accident occurred at this island some four months since, on board nn English ship whilst laying at anchor. The Captain and male having had frequent alter cations, agreed to settle their ditlcieuces on the þÿvessel d s eck with pistols: the carpenter

'll f >11 Ml l-TiTlT-tl r þÿ - il ST measured off the distance with hi rule, and l assed to the opposite side ol the deck, a little forward of the galley þÿ die parties then fired, the þÿmate I s ml! passing between the legs of the captain into die Sterh of the vessel, hut the þÿcaptain ball s crossed the deck and killed this carpenter dead on the spot, whose body now lies interred on die arid sands of \>$session The principals in the dud have been sent home to England in separate Vessels to await their trial. About SO miles N. \V. of this island are three mote Islands cal led Sharks Penguins and Seal, at the last of which we found some six or eight English vessels taking in Guano which is obtained here in the chasms and fissures of the rocks which have been filled partly bv die petu'dical visits ol the seal in pupping, and shedding seasons, and are also the rookery of the sea fowl which united have been gradually filling these chasms during centuries and centuries past Guano is consequently pure decomposed animal matter as its pungent smell of ammonia plainly indicates, so poweiful is this volatile substance, that we could readily scent it at our anchorage, fully hall a nule distant In some places on this island it is found to the depth of 40 feet and in digging it, immense quantities of bone both sea. and fowl, eie found intermingled with hair, shells, and the refuse of t fie lards. 'I he time il has required to fill the fissuies. and for the deposit to undergo and perfect the natural routine of decomposition is beyond conjecture, a id

would puzzle the most subtle theorist. The Guano on this island is not however of superior quality, but a bout 25 miles to the northward is the island of Ichaboc, one solid mass of pure unadulterated guano, arid which is in ihe most perfect slate of decomposition that countless ages and a fervid sun can effect. '1 his island has evidently been originally a reef, or ledge of rocks slightly elevated above the surface of the water, upon w hich the seal have congregated and the Penguins have made a rookery of, until now it is a bed of Guano about half a mile in circumference, anO from fifty to eightv feet in þÿdepth in form lesemlduig a tea cup inverted. We found here a fleet of about 40 sail of English merchant men of the largest class, all in quest of Guano j and i presume as munv more were on their passage to and from Ihe island. In obtaining this guano ; stages are indispensably necessary formed of the spars of vessels and temporarily planked over, of which there are some 15 or 20; down these stages the Guano is carried by the crews of the diflerent vessels in bags, and thrown into their boats, it is then boated off to their respective vessels and in this manner they are loaded The difierent portions, or pits as thev stile them þÿ some a little further advanced than the others, present the appearance of a huge fortress, with all its ramparts and abutments each party as they work, leaving their walls perpendicular, and so hard is the substance that they are compelled to use not onlv the

pick axe. but the beetle and wedge. The skins of seals and birds are found protruding through from top to bottom, also the eggs of the sea fowl some of which 1 have taken 00 feet beneath the surface in a perfect state of preservation. Joliaii. hv the li< v'd Abbe Waal in the Koiuan Catholic. Church of (Justavia (St. Bartholomew ) to a tiuiueroiis congregation, who appeared to evince all the svmpathv to he expected on so melancholy an occasion: "On! Death where is thv sung? þÿ Oh! grave whe-e is thy victory, St. Paul 1 Cor. 15 At 20 Verse., Blessed are liiev who die in the Lord. We see at every moment Dear Chris tian<;, the irrevocable deciees of Divine Providence. taking place in an impartial manner towards every member of societv, Kings as well as their subjects are called on in their i ur ri to render an account of their mortal pilgrimage here below before the La r of divine justice. inexplicable are vour decrees O! Lord! mysterious are your ways. Oil this great and memorable occasion public duty Iras imposed on me, the obligation ot celebrating bv prayer llie departure from this lile of the late monarch of the country whom we all smcerelv regret with unfeigned sorrow. Human passions and opinions are levelled in the dust, all ranks have come forward wiiii one unanimous sentiment of bewailing the departed Sovereign. You have all been the subjects of his late Majesty and as such offer Up yaur prayers at the common altar of mercy. Under this roof consecrated to the service of our common God. No subject is more worthy of the meditation of a christian orator, or of the serious consideration of a christian auditory.

But in this day of public mourning, in this great solemnity of public grief, eloquence should cede iis place to internal feeling and sentiment. Weep tfien mv brethren for your departed King, so worthy of your teais to mourn for whom you are so religiously and nationally assembled this day. We ofler then to the Almighty our tribute of grief and admiration for the late Charles John the XI V , King of Sweden and Norway and of this island. In opening the pages of History, we there see a life replete with great and noble actions. Raised Irom the ranks of his country to the highest honours of the Empire þÿ he distinguished himself in every function, with honotlr and integrity. A great statesman as well as a distinguished Soldier amongst t tie great and extraordinary characters of that remarkable and in all human probability, never again to be equalled epoch. Honoured by the Consular and Imperial Governments þÿ beloved by the soldiery as one of the bravest spirits of the martial eiain which lie lived þÿ and loved and honoured bv the citizens as a true and sincere patriot, it is not extraordinary therefore that possessing such qualifications, a brave! and an indepen dent nation! should inviie him to govern them. And to tile eternal glorv of the memory of the illustrious departed he it þÿSaid that he devoted his best energies, whilst on tlit throne ol Sweden to protect and advance

the interests of his adopted country. In j8(lfl a revolution was i fleeted in Sweden which history has consecrated as an act of tin noun I justice, and which Providence permits in order that such sad and deplorable events may serve as lessons to riders, ii was a complete regeneration, arid was consummated without bloodshed It is foreign to the theme of this, too brief panegvric, to dwell on the causes of this sudden revolution, let it sudice to say þÿ the Swedish Diet in 1800 established the nation in all its rights and privileges and in 1810 called iii a new dvnnstv hv naming this celebrated deceased wuinor as Grown Prince of the country. In 1818 he commenced his reign so justly celebrated in ihe annals of humanity for having secured to Ins eountrv the blessings of peace tor 26 years It was during that happy tranquillity thai order was re established in llie Swedish finances, the army re-organized, magnificent roads constructed and t tie greatest impulse given In trade and agriculture The Capital as well as the conritrv benefitted amazingly bv his presence dm ing his long feign, tor under his auspices, splendid public buildings were erected which render Stockholm at the present day one of the finest cities of Europe; arid we ourselves me we riot indebted to ihe Monarch's liheialnv tor the construction of our church? now an ornament to this island þÿ Let our hopes now he in the Lord, "that he is now receiving the reward of a virtuous life" and that his son "King Oscar the successor to the Throne

and dignities, may inherit the ta'ents and virtues of his ever-to be lamented site. May Divine Providence he his guide in the dangers and perplexities of Itegal þÿlife May he lit; the fallier of his people þÿ rheir protector and defender; þÿ May God protect the new King þÿ give him strength and fortitude in his new and elevated station and may the God of Justice defend a country which has so noblv fought ami bled for independence. Mav our prayers ascend this dav as incense to t lit: I lirotie of mercv for the Swedish nation. May the blessings of our Lord Jesus fie upon you ail now and for evermore. þÿ Amen. Nearly all the known properties of light seem to contradict our best established opinions respecting the laws of motion, and ate frequently opposed to the primary evidence of the sense of sight itself; vet. they are proved by demonstration, so clear as not to admit the shadow of a doubt. When we lied, therefore, the results of human experience with regard to tangible matter, to lie completely inapplicable to so subtle a property as light ; bow much more diffident ought we to bo in drawing conclusions from the observed operations of material substances respecting an essence so inscrutable as that of mind ! and i! in the former ease our deductions itom ordinary experience are fallacious, the objection to any presumed operation state or of ex stenc.c of the mind, founded on no other basis than that ot its supposing opposition to common cxpcii

Invert succeeding discovery, indeed, trenches upon I lie terriioi y of presumed impossibilities, and shows liiat the operations of nature a e not to he circumscribed by the limits which ihe ignorance of man would impose Hut regardless ol these repealed checks on his presumption, he adheres to litis narrow minded system of reasoning, and wi'J persevere in denying ihe possibility of states of being that cannot from their inscrutable nature he brought to the test of positive proofs, though the arguments hv which these objec. lions are attempted to be supported, are merely a repetition ot those that have been previously refuted in the material world, by the advancing progress oj knowledge.

Hence to infer, fust, that the results of experience in ordinary cases, are not to be taken as the limits of possibility in questions relating to subtle properties ; secondly, that ns we perceive causes constantly operating in the material world, ot the nature of which we can term not the least conception, it is no1 improbable that the still more inscrutable essence of the human sou! may be capable of exerting its energies under circumstances that surpass our comprehension ; and thirdly, that th" separate existence ol tins subtle property of matter, independently ot the matter vvtih win li it ts combined, alfo.ds a close analogy to the separate existence ot the sentient prin ciple distinct from the body which it animates. It is thus that in the piogressot knowledge, phenomena which were once attributed to supernatural agency, are gradually discovered to be conformable to established laws. The investigation ot these laws shows that the whole course oi nature is regulated by fixed and unaltered rules l orgetlul of the gradual steps by which he has risen from a state of ignorant wonder to his present position, and unable to perceive the immense height of the eminence above him, man is apt ignorantly to imagine that he has reached the summit of the hill ot science, when lie lias only surmounted some of the obstructions surrounding its base ; ami it is only when obstacles to his further progress present themselves in forms which lie leels ins inability to master, that he becomes aware there is a

higher ground to he attained, and ddlnulties to be yet encountered, which ins mental constitution cannot overcome. The recollection of the progressive stages of our knowledg , and the consideration that what we at present have acquired is but a small portion ot what is yet to be learned ; and that when we have attained the utmost hounds of human wisdom, there are innumerable objects of research, which the intellectual powers of man are incapable oi grasping,

cnimt be too frequently recalled to mind, for the purpose of checking the vain presumption SO irreconcileable with sound þÿphilosophy that all supposed ellccts which are incomprehensible to our limited faculties must be impossible. To be able to see without the eye. to hear without the ear, to feel without touching the objects of sensation, would, we may venture to assert, have been considered utterlv impossible, if we had not experience of the tact from the effects of imagination and of dreams These facts, we contend, afford direct proof in support of the position before advanced, that the percipient principle is independent of the organs of sense ; and they lead us to infer also, that the materia, oignui. sai ion of the brain, by which the impressions of external must he distinct from the power that receives obcts are conveyed to the mind, and retains those impressions; for it would be impossible otherwise to account for the activity ol the perceptive power during the time that the brain ceases to hold any direct communication wiih the material world. expansive power of that subtle property of matter is exerted. Not only, indeed, is the exercise of the intellectual faculties consistent with immaterial agenev, but we may reasonably inter from the analogies presented during the whole course ot oui investigations, that when the mind is detached iron- matter, it will exert its energies with greater vigour than when fettered by its connexion with the corporeal machine; and that when perceptions are received and reflected on directly bv the mind, without tiie intervention of material organs or material processes, they will be more clear and comprehensive, and that the real nature ami properties of the objects perceived will be divested of that obscurity in which they are involved, when

From some despatches of General Lamori r.iere, the officer in command of the French troops, it appears that an engagement took place on the 30th of May. The aliair was

In the course of a short time the engagum tit became general, and was continued for about an tiour and a half, when the undisciplined hordes of Arabs began to give way, and afterwards took to flight, leaving a large number of dead and wounded on the field of battle. The Morocco cavalry distinguished themselves bv singular dating, and one of them actually dashed through a body of sharpshooters and attacked a captain of Chasseurs. þÿ t he loss on the part of the French was very trilling. The following sketch of the present condition of Morocco, and the causes and prospects of war. possesses some interest at the piesent time : þÿ

Mooador, April 28. þÿ We have still here wars and rumours of wars in immediate perspective; and although the provinces of Sliedma and Hhalia have ! sent up all their disposable forces to be reviewed by Ins Excellency the Governor of this city and which have returned again to their homes, the holy þÿwar against the infidels continues as fiercely as ever to agitate the breasts of all true Mussulmans. þÿ The objects of these warlike preparations are said to be two-fold þÿ to repel an hostile expedition of the Spaniards by sea, and to resist the inroads of the French on tfie northeastern frontier. It is obvious t fiat the French army, whilst contending for t fie tow ns of ihe coast, and protecting their environs, had no time to think of the interior and frontier towns; but as soon as they were established there in quiet possession, if such terms be applicable to their conquest, they cast their eyes beyond, and especially on the frontiers. The lirsi frontier question was with Tunis But the prince of that country, who cun distinguish between a petty power like Sardinia and a first-class power like France, soon enabled the Tunisian and French military authorities to come to something like a settlement of their þÿ boundary þÿquestion. Far other, wise is it with Morocco. This government, swollen to a gigantic pride and overweening sell security through the nnlliontimes repealed, but still foolish, dictum that Morocco was certain of the all-powerful support of England, come what might, in any struggle, or in

any war, blindly and furiously, and, we may reasonably suppose, in spite of all the remon" strances of the British Consul, rushes into contest with France, and disputes the line of its north-eastern frontier with that formidable military neighbour. þÿ How far such a contest is agreeable to the personal feelings of the Emperor is another question. It is positively stated here by the most intelligent and respectable Moors, that such a war is quite against the Imperial mind ; that the Emperor dreads Abdel Kader, and Ins aid and unseasonable zeal, more than the French, or any European power, for this indomitable Arab chief obliges him to go to war with France to show his subjects that be is as zealous against the infidels as himself, and equally merits their fanatic admiration ; army and that of the Emperor of Morocco. þÿ and that, moreover, a vast deal of discontent pervades tfie empire, for although the Empeþÿrot system s is pacific, and his genius mercantile, and his general administration has been for more than 20 years unattended with

, i . . ' any sanguinary executions, yet hi.- system ol rule, nevertheless, carried on in the most mercenary spirit, and by roundabout means, thoroughly and effectually drains t .e pockets of Ins people, and both Moors and Arabs, whose passion for money will make tlirm cut one þÿanother sthroats, find the yoke of tfie present government almost insufferable. 1 have heard the Moors themselves confess that their brethren in Algiers enjoy more security of life and property that in Morocco; and it is believed by some persons well acquainted with this country that the first invaders of their country, were they a respectable people, would be welcomed by all the Jews þÿ a tenth of the whole empire þÿ and a great portion of the Arab and Moorish population. The means taken by the Moorish government to meet the present crisis, if novel to us, are vet the best which they have at their disposal. The Emperor ordered all the disposable forces of the coast from Tangiers to Mogador to be reviewed, and provided with new arms, where wanting. The troops of this city were commanded to exchange their old aims for new. All the wealthy Mussulmans in the country were commanded, as an act of piety, to provide arms for their poorer neighbours. The Governor, having collected before him all the tioops of Mogador, haiangued them in this style: þÿ þÿ The infidels are coming; you must prepare to fight them; and you must not fear them, for you ate tetter than they, and God is greater than all þÿ! þÿ

In this wav their courage is brought up to the sticking place of religious fanaticism þÿ The next day after the Governor delivered this anti-infidel speech, the Ftench Consul, M. Jorelie, went to hint and remonstrated against his exciting the natives against the Christian residents of the city Whilst the new levies were lounging about in and out of the city (the greater pari not being permuted to come in), a Christian could not walk out without being cursed and spat upon ; and the Governor at last became so sensible of the folly of his exciting the troops, that he sent round to the consuls to tell them not to let their subjects go out of the city gates until! the levies returned to their homes. T he French consul, for two or thiee weeks, as also myself, never went out of our houses þÿ These levies of troops were at times drawn up outside of the city in one unbroken immense line, the cavalry in the middle, and the infantry on both sides. 1 did not see any artillery. Their firing and praciice were wretched, many of the matchlocks missing fire. Whilst charging, which lasts some six or eight minutes, they sing þÿ God is þÿgreat &c. Besides þÿ playing at þÿpower. which is firing on horseback at full gallop, thes: were their own military manoeuvres. Their war cry is þÿ ha, ha, ha !' pronounced with terrible guttural sounds and screatnings, whilst their faces look as terrible as they can make them. In their grand sham fights, it is usual to divide the troops into Mussulmans and Christians,

altering a little the dress to distinguish them. On one occasion the þÿ þÿmock Christians ran down the þÿ þÿtine Mussulmans, and this was considered an evil omen The amount of the levies of the province of Shedna and Hhalia (provinces of middling size), were about 120,000, but it must be recollected that every ablebodied Moor Arab is considered a soldier. T he raw levies from the country ate many of them barley prepared in dillereut wavs; and it is said that when their barley was consumed, they returned home to their huts nr tents, for the government neither gave them bread nor money.

Some time since we caller the attention of our renders to this truly wonderful instrument, the invention of a Lady Brooklyn ;Mrs Sarah P. Mather) and we are gratified in beinsi aide to stale that vigorous measures are in train to bring its advantages properlv to the attention of the Navy Department and the Congress. On Saturday evening Inst an examination into its capabilities was made by the Commandant of the Navy Yard, several naval officers, and a number of scientific gen tlemen The result of their examination and experiments was their unqualified assent to the advantages claimed to be derived from tts use, and they have made a report to the Navy Department, speaking in the highest terms of its admirable qualities, and recommending the Department to endeavour to procure an appropriation to test it by still further experiments, and to bring it into practical use By the experiments made, it was shown that by means of an ordinary camphire lamp, placed in a glass globe sunk in the water, sufficient light would he given to enable a person standing on the deck of a ship, to examine distinctly every portion of ihe ship's hull, even to the smallest nails used in fastening the coppering. Thus a ship at her moorings may undergo as ihorougti an examination as though she were hauled up into a di v dock, (of course at an immense saving of itme, expense, and in case ol leakage, or Other damage to a vessel while at sea.) the officer standing on deck can at a glance satisfy himself of the precise nature and

extent of the difficulty- It will thus be seen how often, by timely warning and lepair, and that often too under circumstances where there would be no other possible means of ascertaining the facts, many a noble ship with tue lives of those on board of them, might have been preserved from the destruction that otherwise awaited them. But the pnweis of this instrument may fie easily increased so as to produce much more wondeiful lesults. By ihe application ol the Drummond '.,ight to ttie apparatus, even in water as turbid as that ot the Mississipi river, the vision may be thrown at least to the depth of 'djO h et, lighting up a suiface of 500 sq. feet, and in a clear water increasing ihe hundreds to thousands, bringing the smallest object within its range distinctly before the eve þÿ And it does not slop even here in revealing the treasures and ihe mysteries of the deep. If it is desirable or necessary to bring minute objects inme distinctly wnhm the range of vision, magnifying instruments of anv required power may he added to the submarine telescope with the same facility as to an astronomical observation, thus increasing its power to an almost illimitable extent. from what we have said it will fie seen that this instrument may he applied with great advantage to other purposes beside the examination of the hulls ol vessels. In discovering and raising wiecks and other proþÿperty. in removing obstruction in rivers and harbors, and ascertaining their precise nature and locality þÿ in prosecuting the pearl

fisheries, and in fine, the thousand wavs in which marine. explorations may he turned to the most profitable or useful account, its advantages to science, to navigation, 6cc-, me uluiasi incalculable. If the subject be taken

3 V, ------ CHOIS þÿ A T It up by Congress in a properly liberal spirit, and its advantages are developed in scientific experiments, it is not perhaps too much to say that it will be shown to be one of the most important inventions of the age. Front the approbation it has received from the great number of scientific and naval men who have examined it, and the results shown by actual experiment, there would seem to be hardly room for objection from the proper authorities to give it a fair trial, and we leel confident that after such a trial the department would never suffer a ship to leave port without being provided with one of these instruments, so immense would be the saving of expenditure and the increase of safety. The whole appatatus is exceedingly simple arid compact, and not at all likely to get out of repair, and in the high commendations we have bestowed upon it, we use but the unanimous language of those eminently qualified to judge correctly of its merits þÿ New l urk Express. þÿ ooo « þÿ From the Magnet for 1844.

Mr. Editor. þÿ 1'ieitse insert the following for the benefit of the curious and the sceptical in ihe modern science. Dr. Joseph Shreve, a resident and practitioner of meuiome in this village, during the last ten years, aged 50 years, and possessing a predominance of the nervous temperament, has had a small speck or lump under the cuticle a little to the right of i he raplia, or centre ot the under lip, and upon the epithelium, or smooth part. Within the last few mouths, it speedily assumed a cancerous appearance; grew rapiuly, discharged a watery fluid, and caused slight laemating pains, precisely of the character of incipient sclinrhus, or cancer. Having attained the slice ol a large bean, and involving some of the surrounding parts, he liecame uneasy, and resolved to have it removed by excision. A mesmeric sleep w as proposed as a relief from the pain ot the ope atiou. To this lie readily consented, as he was always exceedingly sensitive to any kind ol pain. On the 6th of December, 1843, about 4 o ciock, 1. M , after an operation, by a gentleman of the village, of an hour and three quaiters, he appeared in a profound triesmeiic sleep ; and being sealed in a chateau a composed attitude with folded hands, Dr. C. And how lias tins been done? with what means have these works been wrought out ? This, more than all, declares the greatness of the human mind. Mark that this, pale laced man, who sits out there under die night skies. The li uncial embarrassments of this country are now gtenter than ever they were. In this distressing situation, the first thought of Baron Tojal and his colleagues was to issue Five per Cent. Inscriptions to the amount of 2000 contos, which, being unsupported by any sort of guarantee, would be precisely the same thing as the assignats of the French revolutionary government. For this purpose, an order was sent to the Board of Pub-
